title: Horizontal Scaling and Statelessness: Why Any Instance Must Be Able to Serve Any Request
objective: Explain why statelessness is the property that actually enables horizontal scaling, why sticky sessions quietly break that property, and how pushing session state into a shared backing service restores true interchangeability between instances.

content_blocks.heading: Horizontal Scaling's Real Limit Isn't Hardware
content_blocks.body:
Horizontal scaling adds more identical instances behind a load balancer instead of making one instance bigger (vertical scaling). In principle this looks unbounded -- just keep adding more machines -- but in practice it only works if a request can land on any instance interchangeably and get a correct response regardless of which one actually handles it.

That interchangeability is the real constraint, not the number of machines available. A system where some instances know things other instances don't -- a user's shopping cart sitting only in the memory of the one server that happened to handle their last request -- can't actually use additional instances to absorb more load for that user, no matter how many new instances get added to the pool.

This session covers why that interchangeability property is called statelessness, what specifically breaks it, and how to restore it once it's been quietly lost -- the actual mechanics behind "just add more servers" working in practice, not just in theory.

content_blocks.heading: Statelessness: the Property That Makes Interchangeability Possible
content_blocks.body:
The Twelve-Factor App methodology states the underlying rule directly: a stateless, share-nothing process never assumes anything cached in its own memory or disk will still be there on a future request, because that future request will often land on a completely different process. Any data that genuinely needs to persist belongs in a shared backing service -- typically a database -- not in any individual process's own local state.

This is what actually makes horizontal scaling work: if no instance holds anything unique, every instance is a perfect substitute for every other one, and the load balancer can route any request to whichever instance happens to be free without needing to know or care about that request's history.

The principle generalizes past HTTP request handling too -- the same reasoning applies to background workers (module 24's territory): a stateless worker can pick up any job from the queue, since nothing about a specific job depends on which worker instance happens to process it.

exercises.prompt: According to the Twelve-Factor App's processes guidance, why shouldn't an application rely on data cached in a process's own memory being available on a later request?

options: A later request will often land on a different process, which has no access to the first process's own memory at all
In-memory caching is always slower than reading from a database, making it not worth using for any purpose whatsoever
Process memory is wiped automatically between every single request a server handles, no matter how load balancing works
This guidance only applies to disk storage specifically -- in-memory caching across requests is actually considered safe
definition.explanation: With multiple instances behind a load balancer, there's no guarantee a later request from the same client lands on the same process that handled an earlier one -- so anything cached only in that one process's memory is invisible to whichever instance actually handles the next request.

content_blocks.heading: Sticky Sessions: the "Fix" That Quietly Breaks the Model
content_blocks.body:
Sticky sessions route a given user's requests back to the same specific instance every time, typically to work around that instance holding the user's session data in its own memory. The Twelve-Factor methodology treats this directly as a violation of the stateless-process principle, not a legitimate workaround -- it reintroduces exactly the problem statelessness exists to avoid: that one instance now uniquely matters for that user, and the load balancer can no longer treat instances as interchangeable for them.

The practical consequences follow directly from module 4's process-isolation content: an in-memory cache is private to the one process holding it, so if that specific instance crashes or gets scaled down, every user whose session was "stuck" to it loses their session data entirely -- a single point of failure that horizontal scaling was supposed to eliminate, reintroduced by the very mechanism meant to patch around state that shouldn't have been kept in memory in the first place.

exercises.prompt: A system uses sticky sessions to route each user back to the same instance that holds their in-memory session data. What real problem does this reintroduce?

options: A single point of failure for each user -- if their specific instance crashes, their session data is lost entirely
No real problem at all; sticky sessions are a fully equivalent, interchangeable alternative to a shared backing store
Sticky sessions actually improve fault tolerance, since each user's data is now protected by being isolated to one instance
The load balancer itself becomes unable to route any traffic at all once sticky sessions are enabled for any user
definition.explanation: Sticky sessions make one specific instance uniquely load-bearing for each user's session -- exactly the single point of failure horizontal scaling across interchangeable instances is meant to eliminate. If that one instance crashes or is removed, every session stuck to it is lost, since the data only ever existed in that one process's own memory.

content_blocks.heading: The Actual Fix: Push Session State Into a Shared Backing Service
content_blocks.body:
Rather than routing requests back to wherever the data happens to be cached, the stateless-process model moves session data into a shared backing service -- a store like Redis or Memcached, accessible identically from every instance -- so any instance can read a user's current session on any request, not just the one that happened to create it. The Twelve-Factor guidance specifically recommends a store with built-in time-based expiration for this, since session data is naturally temporary and benefits from being automatically cleaned up rather than accumulating forever.

This directly restores true interchangeability: every instance becomes a stateless, disposable worker that reads whatever shared state it needs for the current request and writes back whatever changed, with nothing unique living only in any one instance's own memory -- which also means a crashed instance (module 38's resilience territory) can simply be replaced without losing anything, since it never held anything that wasn't also safely stored elsewhere.

exercises.prompt: A team moves session data from in-process memory into a shared Redis store accessible from every instance. What does this change actually restore?

options: True interchangeability between instances -- any instance can now serve any request without needing specific prior history
Nothing meaningful changes in practice; Redis and in-process memory behave identically from the load balancer's perspective
The need for a load balancer entirely, since Redis itself can now route requests directly to the correct instance on its own
Permanent, non-expiring storage for session data, which the team would otherwise have no reasonable way to achieve at all
definition.explanation: Once session data lives in a shared backing service every instance can read and write identically, no single instance holds anything unique anymore -- any instance can serve any request for any user, restoring the interchangeability that statelessness is supposed to provide and that in-memory caching had quietly broken.

content_blocks.heading: A Concrete Comparison: Shopping Cart in Memory vs. in Redis
content_blocks.body:
A shopping cart kept only in the memory of the instance that created it works fine until the load balancer happens to route that user's next request to a different instance -- at which point the cart appears empty, since the new instance never saw it. The exact same cart stored in Redis instead is visible identically from every instance, so the user's next request lands correctly no matter which instance actually handles it, and the cart survives even if the original instance is scaled down or crashes entirely.

Worth noting: moving the cart into Redis doesn't eliminate distributed-systems concerns -- it just relocates them. Module 36's replication and consistency content still applies to whatever store now holds that shared state; the problem of coordinating state across machines hasn't disappeared, it's been concentrated into one well-understood, purpose-built shared service instead of being scattered unpredictably across every application instance's own memory.

exercises.prompt: After moving a shopping cart from in-process memory into Redis, does this fully eliminate the distributed-systems concerns this module has covered?

options: No -- it relocates those concerns into one shared store, where module 36's replication and consistency content still applies
Yes, completely -- Redis is fully immune to every distributed-systems concern this module has covered, including replication
No, Redis is actually less reliable overall than keeping the cart in each individual application instance's own memory
This question doesn't really apply here, since Redis itself isn't considered a real distributed system in any meaningful way
definition.explanation: Moving shared state into Redis solves the specific interchangeability problem this session covers, but Redis itself is still a system that has to make its own replication and consistency choices (module 36's territory) -- the coordination problem doesn't vanish, it's concentrated into one well-understood shared service rather than scattered unpredictably across application instances.

content_blocks.heading: The Bottom Line
content_blocks.body:
Horizontal scaling only actually works if any instance can serve any request interchangeably, and statelessness -- keeping no request-specific data in a process's own memory or disk -- is the property that makes that interchangeability possible, per the Twelve-Factor App's own processes guidance. Sticky sessions look like a reasonable workaround for in-memory session data, but they quietly reintroduce the exact single-point-of-failure problem horizontal scaling exists to eliminate. The real fix is pushing that shared state into a backing service every instance can read and write identically, which also makes a crashed instance trivially replaceable, directly connecting to module 38's resilience content.

The next sessions in this module build on this stateless-instance foundation directly: partitioning and sharding data itself across machines, service discovery for finding which instances exist right now, leader election and distributed scheduling, multi-region design, and consistent hashing as the specific technique that avoids hotspots when distributing both data and traffic.
